headline_hi: समुद्र तट के कचरे से बेंच
summary_en: People have done a wonderful job at Mumbai's Dadar Beach. Over fifteen hundred volunteers joined together here to run a massive cleanup drive. With several hours of hard work, everyone collected eighteen thousand kilograms of waste. A very large portion of this waste removed from the beach was plastic. Now, this entire waste plastic is being given a new life. By recycling this plastic, school benches will be made for underprivileged children. This will give children good seating facilities in classrooms for studying. At the same time, the beach can be kept clean from plastic pollution and filth. Organizers believe that real change comes from segregating waste daily. If we do not throw trash on the beach, the shores will always remain clean. This responsibility of citizens is a very good lesson for both society and the environment. This campaign shows that a big change can be brought with the right mindset.

lead.title: From Beach Plastic to School Benches
lead.summary: Mumbai’s beaches gave us 18,000+ kg of waste. But what if this waste could give children a better future? :ocean::recycle: Over 1,500 volunteers joined The Better India’s Civic Sense Revolution at Dadar Beach, turning hours of hard work into a powerful reminder: change begins when we take responsibility. The collected plastic can be transformed into school benches for underprivileged students, giving discarded waste a second life. But the real revolution? A day when our beaches don’t need cleaning because we stop littering, segregate waste, and practise civic sense every day. headline_hi: बाढ़ पीड़ितों के लिए फोल्डेबल घर
summary_en: Severe floods in Chennai snatched away the makeshift homes of many families. Relief arrived immediately after the floods, but building permanent houses takes years. Shreeram Ravichandran, a student at IIT Madras, understood this serious problem deeply. He saw that there is a long wait between relief tents and permanent houses. To ease this very difficulty, he began working with his team. These engineering students developed special foldable and modular buildings. These buildings can be easily set up in places where construction is difficult. So far, their organization has built more than fifteen hundred such modular buildings. This technology helps provide an immediate safe roof to homeless families. With this remarkable ingenuity of the students, a new hope has been sparked in the lives of disaster victims. This step taken in difficult times is truly inspiring for everyone.

lead.title: From Hostel Room Model to 1500+ Foldable Buildings: IIT Grads Build Infrastructure That Travels
lead.summary: This article has been published in partnership with Kalaari Capital. Five weeks after the Chennai floods, most of the volunteers had gone home. In the first few days, help had seemed to come from everywhere. People arrived with food, water and relief material. Among them was Shreeram Ravichandran, then a second-year civil engineering student at IIT Madras with Engineers Without Borders. As the weeks passed, he began noticing something the first rush of relief could not solve. In settlements between Chennai’s OMR and ECR, homes made of thatch had been washed away. Families had lost belongings and the spaces they had lived in, sometimes within hours. “Within just moments, you lose your complete home and all your belongings. Everything is gone,” he recalls. Modulus later developed modular buildings for places where conventional construction is difficult.   The floods had affected Shreeram too, but differently. His neighbourhood faced power cuts and interruptions in food supply. The building he lived in remained standing. “For these people, they just didn’t know what they were going to do the next week or the next day, where they would stay,” he says. “It had just become empty land.” Long after the water receded, that difference stayed with him. Relief could arrive within days. A permanent house could take years. What was a family supposed to do in between? The years between a tent and a home Back at IIT Madras, Shreeram and his fellow students began trying to understand that gap. They looked at what had happened after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and found that permanent rehabilitation could stretch across several years. headline_hi: प्लास्टिक मुक्त स्कूल की अनोखी पहल
headline_en: Unique Initiative for a Plastic-Free School
summary_en: In a school in Singapore, students ran a unique campaign against plastic pollution. There, two thousand students used to use seventy-two thousand plastic items every year. To stop this, fifteen to sixteen-year-old children launched a major campaign. They promoted reusable lunch boxes instead of disposable containers. Their effort won the first prize in the Unplastify Challenge 2026. This international program is running in four hundred schools across twenty-five countries. So far, three thousand students together have saved seventy-two tons of plastic. In Chile, children developed an eco-friendly glitter powder. Meanwhile, in Costa Rica, natural loofah was used instead of plastic sponges. Young people in Turkey have researched eco-friendly gloves for hospitals. These small ideas of students are protecting nature worldwide today. The hard work of these children shows that change can begin from school.

lead.title: Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis
lead.summary: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. headline_hi: ऑस्ट्रेलिया में सोलर एनर्जी का रिकॉर्ड
summary_en: A huge historic record has been set in the clean energy sector in Australia. There, on Saturday, solar and wind energy generated more than eighty percent of the electricity. During the afternoon, more than half of the electricity was produced solely from rooftops of homes. Across the country, more than forty-three lakh families have installed solar panels. These rooftop panels together met half of the grid's demand on their own. The rest of the electricity was generated from large solar plants, wind turbines, and hydro projects. During this period, the share of fossil fuels like coal and gas remained at just twenty percent. The surplus electricity was securely stored in pumped hydro storage and large batteries. Experts say that several such new records could be set in the coming weeks. This success proves that clean energy can power the entire country.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: Australia sets a new renewable energy record, with rooftop solar leading the way
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM On Saturday, September 22, solar and wind met 80.4 percent of demand on Australia’s national electricity market, with the grid covering the eastern states, South Australia, and the Australian Capital Territory. For about 30 minutes around lunchtime, rooftop panels on homes and businesses across the country carried more than half of the total load by themselves. Large-scale solar and wind farms covered most of the rest, with hydro adding around one percent. Fossil fuels accounted for 20 percent. Rooftop solar as a grid-scale contributor More than 4.3 million Australian households now have rooftop solar installed. Saturday’s record showed what those installations add up to in practice: enough distributed generation to carry the country through the middle of the day without needing much from the main grid at all. Energy Minister Chris Bowen called it “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before,” and said more records should be expected as the transition continues. Why these records will keep falling Dr. Dylan McConnel l, an energy systems researcher at the University of New South Wales, called it “record season” for renewables. The conditions helped: clear sunny days, low demand from heating and cooling, and timing that landed right as a full year of new generation capacity came online all at once. “These records are probably not going to last very long,” McConnell said. “They’re probably going to be broken in the next couple of weeks.” Some of the surplus went into pumped hydro storage and batteries. headline_hi: अस्पतालों में शोर घटाने की तकनीक
headline_en: Technology to Reduce Noise in Hospitals
summary_en: The noise of machines in hospital wards has always been a major problem. In ICUs, this noise often ranges between fifty to seventy decibels, which is as loud as heavy traffic. Many times, it even reaches one hundred decibels. This is far higher than the thirty-decibel level set by the World Health Organization. In a single shift, staff have to hear hundreds of alarms. Ninety percent of these alarms are such that require no medical intervention. To tackle this problem, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust in the United Kingdom took an initiative in the year 2023. They launched a three-year Silent Hospital pilot project. In this, an attempt is being made to route sound like data. The results of its second phase have been quite good. Now, other hospitals in the UK are also preparing to adopt it.

lead.title: The Hospital That Silenced the Machines
lead.summary: B eep. Beep. Beep. The heartbeat monitor chirps. Hospitals have long tried to fight acoustic chaos with passive tactics — hanging sound-absorbing ceiling tiles, laying soft rubber flooring or begging clinical staff to whisper in the corridors. Beep. Beep. Beep. Blood pressure drops. But the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust in the United Kingdom has been trying something different. Instead of regarding noise as an inevitable physical nuisance that needs to be muffled, it treats sound as data that can be routed. In 2023, the trust launched the Silent Hospital Pilot Project , a three-year study exploring how to target “alarm fatigue” and noise pollution on hospital wards. As the second phase of the pilot comes to an end, its outcomes have already been so promising that other hospital networks around the U.K. are preparing to follow suit. Beep. Beep. Beep. Oxygen levels dip. Hospital wards are notoriously loud, with continuous background noise on intensive care units , for example, often averaging 50 to 70 decibels (dB), comparable to heavy traffic, and sharp peaks frequently passing 80 to 100 dB, roughly the equivalent of a jackhammer. These levels vastly exceed the World Health Organization’s recommended threshold of 30 dB to be able to rest. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. The monitor escalates to an urgent, repeating multi-tone musical sequence engineered to demand immediate human attention. Studies across international health systems reveal that clinical staff encounter hundreds of alarm signals per shift, up to 90 percent of which require no clinical intervention, for example because a patient mistakenly presses the buzzer when they move. headline_hi: मूँगे की चट्टानों को मिली सुरक्षा
summary_en: A new way has been found to protect coral reefs from warm ocean water. Scientists placed floating shades over brain coral in the ocean of Florida. These shades were made from PVC frames and nylon mesh. They were floated in the water about twelve inches, or thirty centimeters, above the coral. The natural color of twenty coral colonies under the shades began returning rapidly. Meanwhile, other reefs without shades were losing their color from the harsh sun rays. These shades do not cool the water, but rather block the sun's ultraviolet rays. Nova Southeastern University scientist Karen Neely described this research as very significant. This technique proved effective in providing immediate protection to fragile coral in extreme heat. This successful experiment has raised hopes of saving marine life across the world.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: How a floating shade can help coral survive a marine heatwave
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM When divers installed floating shade structures over 20 colonies of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys in August 2024, the corals underneath began recovering their color. The 20 colonies left unprotected grew paler through the hottest stretch of the season. That was during 2024’s second-highest heat stress year on record at the site since 1985. The results appear in Frontiers in Marine Science . The shades were made from PVC frames and nylon mesh, suspended roughly 12 inches (30 centimeters) above the coral. They weren’t cooling the water. They were blocking the intense sunlight and ultraviolet radiation that amplifies heat-related bleaching. Why Florida’s 2023 heatwave made this study necessary In the summer of 2023, a record marine heatwave hit the Florida Keys. At most monitored sites, every kind of coral bleached. Branching corals, including the staghorn and elkhorn species, were nearly wiped out. At one inshore location, more than half of the corals researchers were tracking lost some or all their living tissue. Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, the study’s lead author, described the umbrella project as a direct response. “This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” she said. “ Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide. Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.” The scale of the global bleaching crisis Scale is where the Florida experiment runs into its limits. headline_hi: खेती के कचरे से साफ़ गैस
summary_en: A large plant to produce clean energy from agricultural waste has started in Italy. This new biomethane plant has been set up in an area named Grottole in southern Italy. Here, an excellent alternative to natural gas will be produced from crop residues. This plant will produce forty-five gigawatt-hours of renewable energy every year. This electricity and gas will meet the needs of more than three thousand homes. This will lead to a massive reduction of nine thousand tons of carbon dioxide emissions every year. This proper use of waste is a fantastic way to protect the environment from pollution. The company described this entire project as a major step toward a green future. Clean fuel reaching every home from farmers' discarded waste is a very pleasant thing. This model shows that clean energy needs can be met even from waste.

lead.title: Italian Bio-methane Plant Comes Online, Providing Renewable Gas to Over 3,000 Homes
